utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have the case called [Realtime transcript read in error "Tiff I have the case called"], please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see that this is going to be a heated session, because it says "tiff, I have the case called." So good morning, Mr. Brdjanin. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down, thank you. General Talic, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can hear in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner plus Denise Gustin for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, both of you. And appearances for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman, and I appear today with Tania Radosavljevic. My co-counsel, Ms. Maglov, has returned to Banja Luka to do some things there important to this case, and she'll return when she gets those completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman and good morning to you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I am Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic, assisted by Fabien Masson, and I represent General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci, we can start and [French phrase]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I deal very swiftly. I know Mr. Ackerman wants to raise a couple of matters -- with the matter that Your Honour raised at the end of Friday's session, which related to the apparent difference between the wording in document -- it's P227, I think. I'll just remind myself -- which is the first set of Crisis Staff gazette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, 227. And Your Honour drew attention to the difference in the wording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The decision shall come into force on the day it is issued."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And on the next one: "The decision shall come into effect on the day it is adopted." Your Honour, after court, I had someone who reads and speaks the Bosnian language read through the original. Your Honour, it can be dealt with through the witness, if necessary. But the wording in the original is identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It would appear that one translator - and both of these are final translations - has decided to use the word "issued," and the other "adopted." And that, I'm afraid, is one of the problems about translation is that it's very much a question of what word the translator decides to use. But in fact, in the original, it's identical, the word used. But I imagine that Mr. Dzonlic can deal with that. Your Honour, the second matter is Your Honour asked for whether we had the statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Your Honour, we do. It's already been produced and admitted into evidence. It is Exhibit P80, and it's in the first volume of the Banja Luka documents. If Your Honours have it with you, it's divider 27, I think, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm. I thank you, Ms. Korner. Anything else? Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two matters, and I hope neither will prolong -- delay our getting to the witness, because I don't intend it to be that way. The first one is I was reminded, I think, by Ms. Korner on Friday that time has passed when I told you I would file my updated pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have forgotten that. And I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Chamber hasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sure you haven't, Your Honour. There are two possibilities: One, the impetus for the order was a motion filed by the Prosecutor, and it's the position of Ms. Korner that she's really not interested in having me file that document with regard to the law. I suspect, however, the Chamber might be, in spite of that. If the Chamber is, I would then ask -- it will take me about two days full time, I think, to do it, and I haven't found two days to do it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long did it take you to file the motion on Rule 90?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I spent about six hours working on that motion, Your Honour. But that was a matter of immediate moment in the case, I thought. And the issue of what the law is regarding various matters in this case really won't come into play until the motion for judgement of acquittal at the close of the Prosecutor's evidence, I would think. But in any event, I will do as the Chamber directs me to do, although there's evidence that I didn't when you directed me last time. If you would like me to -- well, what I would prefer to do, if you want me to file it, is to do it after the March break, because I'll have that period of time in which I can do it right and do it properly. If you want me to do it more quickly than that, then I will, but other parts of my duties may suffer as a result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, our interest, as Your Honour may recall, was that we got rather more clarification of what the factual defence was. I -- Mr. Ackerman, I have informed that -- I wouldn't say I wasn't interested, but that I certainly wasn't pushing for any answer on the law. I agree with Mr. Ackerman that it's not likely to arise until the close of the Prosecution's case. So Your Honour, I remain entirely neutral on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A woman's heart is always much more tender than mine. I was prepared to give you until the 3rd of April. They have suggested the 10th of April. So Mr. Ackerman, you have an extension up to the 10th of April. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The next matter is, this weekend, I was working on the Rule 92 bis material with regard to the Sanski Most part of the case. And in that connection, met with Madam Fauveau with regard to it, and there are some problems with 92 bis which I feel I need guidance from the Chamber on - not today - but I would like to tell you what I see as issues that I think need to be resolved and we need to be given some guidance on. And that's this. I've written down four things that I think are important. Does a decision by Defence counsel not to request cross-examination of a 92 bis witness mean that the Chamber will treat that statement then as true? And if not, how will the Chamber assess the weight of a 92 bis statement? If a 92 bis statement is merely cumulative of other evidence, then why should it be admitted at all? And if it relates to a subject that has been contested with other witnesses, live witnesses, as to that subject, may a 92 bis statement be admitted at all? In other words, if the issue is one that is being contested -- let me take for instance, the conditions in a detention facility. There may have been five witnesses who have come and testified about the conditions in that facility. Each of the five have been cross-examined fairly vigorously involving that issue. There are three 92 bis witnesses who say roughly the same thing about the conditions in the camp. By not bringing them for cross-examination, do we then admit that what they say in their statements is correct or must we challenge their testimony the same way we've challenged the witnesses who came here live? And I think before decisions can be made about whether to accept a Rule 92 bis statement without bringing the witness for cross-examination, we need some guidance regarding those issues. And that might take you some time to ponder among the three of you, but I think it's -- I think it's important for us to know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm slightly taken by surprise -- although Mr. Ackerman mentioned it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wonder if -- we seem to be putting off an awful lot of things. We're not trying to keep a list of what we put off. But whether Your Honours would -- if Your Honours want to hear argument or, rather, would like assistance on that, whether Your Honours would delay that to give us a chance to consider those points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean, the answer to the cumulative one, well, of course, I think that was one of the points, because it's under Rule 92 bis (A)(i)(a), where it says: Factors in favour of admitting evidence include, "is of a cumulative nature, in that other witnesses will give or have given oral testimony of similar facts." So the answer to that one would seem very quickly, yes, it is admissible. As to the first question is one to treat it as true, and the third, namely, what's the situation where there has been cross-examination on a particular issue? Your Honour, there are certain provisions that I'm aware of in English law that cover that type of situation, but I think I would -- I'd prefer to have time to consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. The same applies to us. Obviously, this is something that we'd need to discuss amongst ourselves as well. What I suggest -- the approach I suggest is that when more or less you're ready or you are in a position to discuss this, what I suggest is that the two sides meet and present the Chamber with a joint document, articulating the points that you need direction about. There may be, for example, with regard to the cumulative nature, I think what you have already referred to is in itself self-explanatory and maybe we'd drop that with the question of whether this would be considered to be true or not. I think the Trial Chamber will never give you a clear-cut answer "yes," because obviously it will depend from case to case and also on the ensemble of -- but in any case, what I suggest is once you are in a position to debate it or to discuss it, make submissions, I would suggest you make -- draw up this joint document, submit it to the Trial Chamber. In the meantime, we would have thought about the matter as well. And then we will give it an hour or so to discuss it, if necessary, or else if we are prepared to hand down a -- not necessarily a decision, but a directive or direction, we will do that. I think that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would hope we'd be able to reach agreement on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But if not, it may require oral argument and a ruling by Your Honours. Your Honour, as I say, there are a number of matters still outstanding which at some stage I think we better find a morning to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- whenever you like. Whenever you like.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, you are bringing the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You know what the logistical problems are much more, because obviously the Chamber is not kept informed of what is happening. So any time you make a proper suggestion to that effect, we're open. We will be forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, at the moment, Your Honour, there's no question in the near future. We have witnesses stacked up now because it's all taking a lot longer than we anticipated originally. So I would say we've Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. got witnesses here until the middle of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would suppose that it would make sense that this be dealt with sooner rather than later, because someone is going to want to know our view regarding the 92 bis witnesses from Sanski Most, rather soon I would think, rather than two or three weeks from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you, Mr. Ackerman and Ms. Korner. I mean, very rightly, Ms. Korner said she's been taken by surprise, so I would give her all the time she needs, definitely. And when she's ready, I suppose she can sit down together with you and Madam Fauveau, see what's left that really needs the intervention of the Trial Chamber, and we will meet you on that -- on that issue the earliest possible opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know how to raise a new issue without taking someone by surprise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It wasn't a complaint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it's not a complaint. It's not a complaint. It's a fair comment. The same applies for us. We were not prepared for it. So can we call the witness. Let's have the witness inside the courtroom and we'll continue with his cross-examination. Do you anticipate to finish your cross-examination today, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Dzonlic. You are going to be asked once more to read the statement, to tell us the whole truth and nothing but the truth. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down, thank you. Mr. Ackerman, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dzonlic.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to start this morning with kind of a digression, I suppose. There was a time during your direct examination when you talked about some guys who came from Belgrade with a whole bunch of money. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what was that money?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We called those Serbian dinars, and they became the currency. They were new dinars, Serbian dinars, which came from Belgrade, and they were used as the currency in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what I don't understand is did these people just come hand out money to people? Was it just free money?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people didn't hand out money. It wasn't them. They had with them large amounts of that money. And as I said, they used it to pay for things in the pizzeria, in the restaurant. They paid the expenses, and they said that they had brought the money in a convoy of armoured vehicles and that this was the kind of money that would be the currency used in the future. And they said that the same kind of money -- that they were taking the same sort of money to the Serbian Krajina, to Knin in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. You told us all those same things before. The question was: Was it just free money? Did they just hand it out to people? I think your answer is no.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say they handed out the money to people. I said they used it to pay their expenses, to pay for drinks. They treated people and paid in that money. They didn't give money, as such. I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the money was put into circulation in Banja Luka by these guys doing a lot of drinking and eating a lot of pizzas and paying for it? Is that how it got into circulation?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not the way it came into circulation. What I said was that they used that money to pay for things, and they said that they used transporters, armoured vehicles, to bring in huge amounts of that money. I didn't see those vehicles myself, but they said that they were bringing large amounts of money. I assumed they were taking that money to the financial institutions because all the financial transactions went through the SDK, the public accountancy service, and they took the money there, I assume, and that's where it was stored.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you think it was just put into banks?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That service, the SDK, it's a service for payments. It's not a bank. Payment settlement, that's what it does. And daily payments were balanced there. And after a certain amount of time, certainly, that money must have reached the banks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There were dinars in circulation in Banja Luka from World War II up to that time, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were dinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what you're talking about is the new dinar -- what was called the new dinar; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was now a new currency, a new form, a new appearance of the bank notes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know, do you not, that the new dinar did not come into circulation until January 1, 1994?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you deny it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the new dinar entered into circulation in 1994? I said that I didn't know that, the fact it had entered circulation in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. When we broke on Friday, we were talking about the relative competencies of the Executive Council of ARK, headed by Nikola Erceg, and the Crisis Staff of ARK. And I had put to you the question that since Mr. Erceg was the person who had appointed the Crisis Staff, then he would necessarily have maintained superior position over the Crisis Staff and could have removed anyone that he had appointed to that Crisis Staff at any time. The next place I want to direct your attention is to -- it's clear, is it not, that Mr. Erceg remained in his position and continued to operate in his position as president of the Executive Council of the Autonomous Region of Krajina after the appointment of the Crisis Staff? You agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't have your documents in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could I get Prosecution Exhibit 227 brought to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. If I may, before I answer any other question, may I say that as far as I was able to understand, the last time I was examined, the statement that I gave would be given to me here in front of me. So that was my understanding, that I could have that statement here in front of me. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think he wants his written statement. And I have no objection to that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any objection to that, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's a difference of systems, of course that's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry about that. If you don't see any objection, I will let him have the documents. Obviously, if you are going to refer to any part of that document, he should -- in my jurisdiction, you would read it out or you would let him see that particular part. So I have no objection at all, and -- like we did with previous witnesses, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right. And of course I think that's right. Last time he was given his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because he was asked about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please do. And Mr. Dzonlic, the statement he made on the 5th, 6th and 7th of May, 2001, and the other statement he made on the 11th and 12th of October, 2000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Dzonlic, we are talking about number 5 in Exhibit P227. Number 5 is a decree on organising enterprises from parts of the work process; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I can't find it. I have another decision in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The decision is number 5, Exhibit P227, the decree that is signed by Nikola Erceg, several articles.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And that is dated 9 May 1992, is it not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's four days after the date that Mr. Erceg appointed a Crisis Staff; correct? The Crisis Staff was appointed at document number 2, decision number 2, on 5 May 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this decree is signed by Nikola Erceg as president of the Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the preamble indicates that it is pursuant to article 24, section 2 of the ARK statute?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find that decision. I don't have it. Just a moment, please. Oh, yes. Yes, I see it. I see it. Yes. Yes. Yes, yes. I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the preamble also indicates that there was a session of the Executive Council on May 9th at which this decree was agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to go back one document to conclusion number 4.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This document refers, if you look at the preamble, to a meeting of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina that was held on 8 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the preamble clearly indicates, does it not, that this was a meeting of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 1, at least according to the translation, paragraph 1 refers to information that must be supplied to the war staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Is that what it says in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you look at number 3, it says that: "Presidents of the National Defence Councils are to report to the war staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina"; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you've agreed that this was a meeting of the Crisis Staff. And they're drawing conclusions about things that must be submitted to or reported to the war staff. Do you believe that is a different body, the war staff? Is it different from the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if you look, then, Mr. Dzonlic, at paragraphs 5 and 6. Paragraphs 5 and 6, the Crisis Staff is making requests; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And paragraph 5, they're requesting certain activity on behalf of the military?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And paragraph 6, they're requesting certain activity on behalf of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the reason that the Crisis Staff is using the word "request" is because they have no competence to order either the military or the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to do anything. All they can do is to request. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I ask you to repeat that question again, please? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. The reason the word "request" -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm going to object, Your Honour. I was half minded to anyhow. It's pure comment. We can all read what the word says. The witness can read what the word says. Whether or not they can only request because they have no competence, that's a matter of comment. This witness can't answer that question. All he can do is read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would allow [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would allow the question, Ms. Korner, also because as I read through these documents, I think some sort of clarification from the witness as to whether he sees a distinction between "it's hereby requested" or "presidents of the National Council are to," -- "distribution is to be placed" -- "presidents of the ... are to supply." There is a clear distinction when the Crisis Staff are directing the National Defence Council or other institutions and the JNA and the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There may be a very simple answer to that, to tell you the truth, and I anticipate what the answer could be. But I would rather have the witness say it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I've no doubt that Mr. Ackerman is perfectly right. I mean, one can read that oneself, and it would seem common sense. What I'm querying is, is whether this witness is in a position to do any more than all of us in reading this. That's my only query.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will accept the Prosecution's statement that I'm perfectly right and move forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to move forward now, Mr. Dzonlic, to conclusion number 6. Let me know when you've found number 6.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Again, this refers to the meeting of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And it's the next day. It's now the 9th of May. The last one referred to was the 8th of May, I believe. And on the 9th of May, they arrived at some additional conclusions. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They concluded that the war staff should have a press centre, in paragraph 1; right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the second part of paragraph 2, they concluded that only persons loyal to SRBiH may make decisions on the implementation of general mobilisation in public and economic organisations; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then in the next paragraph, they talk about, "Decisions adopted by the war staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina are to be strictly respected in all public and economic organisations." Yes?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct that the decisions have to be respected by all public and economic organisations, yes. And the word "strictly" is there, must be strictly respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And that paragraph refers to decisions of the war staff, as opposed to conclusions of the Crisis Staff, does it not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are decisions of the war staff of the autonomous region.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look now at paragraph 5. Paragraph 5 is characterised as an appeal to the presidents of the National Defence Councils to take immediate steps to disarm paramilitary formations and individuals who illegally own weapons and ammunition." It refers to illegal ownership of weapons and ammunition, does it not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back for a moment to paragraph 2, where we talked about only persons loyal to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You know, do you not, that in the police ranks, a loyalty oath was presented to police officers to state whether or not they were loyal to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? You're familiar with that loyalty oath. I think you've testified about it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that in the police ranks, 70 per cent of Muslim police signed the oath and 80 per cent of Croatian police signed the oath? Do you believe that to be the case?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, and I don't believe that to be the case in Banja Luka because I know perhaps two policemen who are Muslims who signed this loyalty oath. As for what you have just said, I don't know about that, and I don't believe that those figures are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Under the law, it was perfectly legal, was it not, for an individual to own a hunting weapon if it was properly permitted -- a permit had been properly issued and the law had been followed, it was legal to own a hunting weapon, was it not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was legal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when the appeal or the order or the request or the conclusion is that individuals should turn in illegally owned weapons, that would not have applied to their hunting weapons, would it, that were legally acquired?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's look at decision number 7 now. It's actually conclusion number 7. And this is another meeting of the Crisis Staff held two days later, on May 11th, is it not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And again, in paragraph 1, it speaks of the surrender of illegally acquired weapons, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In paragraph 6, it talks about able-bodied men, aged between 18 and 55, who have fled from the ARK must immediately return. It's the case, isn't it, that a number of Serbs fled from the ARK to avoid mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, may I remind you that you put this question to the witness at least twice last Friday. And he gave you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that should be enough, then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go -- let's go, Mr. Dzonlic, to the next document, number 8. The first thing I want to do is just kind of a review. If you go back through the Crisis Staff meetings of 8 May, 9 May, and 11 May, those documents are all conclusions, are they not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we go to the document at number 8, that's a document that's called a "decision," isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And again, this is a document that is signed by Nikola Erceg?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: President of the Executive Council. And what he's doing in that document is appointing Mr. Brdjanin to yet another position; right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In formal and legal terms, that is right. But in substance, I don't think it was he that appoints him but the Crisis Staff. And in view of the fact that it refers to the secretariat as a body of the Executive Council, the decision is signed by the president of the Executive Council, Mr. Nikola Erceg.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us, I think the first day that you started testifying in this case, that the Crisis Staff basically substituted itself for the Assembly of ARK, and the executive of ARK was the Executive Council, and that it was the job of the Executive Council to implement the conclusions of the Crisis Staff. Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Mr. Erceg, as a person who in the hierarchy of ARK was superior to Mr. Brdjanin, would have had discretion regarding the implementation of the conclusions entered into by the Crisis Staff, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Erceg was at the same time a member of the Crisis Staff, so it's the same people are trying you and the same people are prosecuting you. So you have the same person in several bodies. And so you see, that is illustrative of the way they acted. At the same time, he was president of the Executive Council and a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, can I interrupt for a moment? I missed the way the question was put. It was put: Mr. Erceg as person who in the hierarchy of ARK was superior to Mr. Brdjanin. And -- now, that question was put, I think, on Friday, and I don't think it was agreed to by Mr. Dzonlic, but it's now being asserted as a fact, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I take it it's being put as a question. But certainly what you're stating, that Mr. Dzonlic was very categoric about the power or the status that Mr. Erceg had, yes, you are right. He definitely was very categoric about that, which means that he can definitely answer the question, and he was in the process of answering it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, exactly -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, but my objection is, if one reads the question, it seems to be an assertion of facts, which is not, in our submission, borne out by any evidence that's been given in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not yet. You are perfectly right, Ms. Korner. In that regard, you are perfectly right. So perhaps, Mr. Ackerman, could you rephrase the question, not repeating what you have already asked from the witness last Friday, because you put the question last Friday to have witness explain to you how was it that Mr. Erceg was the president of the Executive Council and as witness was putting it, he did not, however, have any executive power which vested instead in the Crisis Staff. That is what he said last time. And perhaps on the basis of that, since in reality if you look at the -- at the hierarchy -- if you look at the hierarchy, then maybe you are right. I mean, Mr. Erceg would appear on top of the list being the president of the Executive Council. But in essence, what witness has said -- has stated throughout, is that he had no power.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I can go at that a different way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, if you look at all of the Crisis Staff conclusions that we've been talking about this morning, those all came from a session of the Crisis Staff held on different days. That's true, is it not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you told us you don't know who the members of the Executive Council were. You just know that Nikola Erceg was its president.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in line with what you told us about the Crisis Staff concluding and the Executive Council implementing those conclusions as executive decisions, I'd like you to look at conclusion number 9. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And paragraph 8 of that conclusion, which comes from a meeting of the Crisis Staff on 13 May, says that "Radoslav Brdjanin is to be appointed secretary of the secretariat for traffic and communications, construction, and spatial planning, and the fund for highways and regional roads," the important language there being "is to be appointed." In other words, it carries the implication of a recommendation, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you look, then, at the decision of Nikola Erceg of the same day, he did not completely carry out the conclusion of the Crisis Staff, but, using his discretion, made a slightly different decision, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me direct your attention --

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the decisions. I was just going to say the following: Both decisions, or rather, the decision and the conclusion were adopted on the same day, the 13th of May. We don't know which came first, the decision or the conclusion. In my judgement, the decision came first, because he was appointed acting secretary. And after that, the conclusion was adopted to appoint him secretary. So I think that is what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if you're correct that what the Executive Council does is implement the conclusions of the Crisis Staff, then it should be pretty clear that it's the decision that came second and that Mr. Erceg appointed him as acting secretary, rather than as secretary, as the Crisis Staff asked?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should point out they in fact have been copied back to front, because if you look at the numbers, Mr. Ackerman is correct. I don't want anybody to go from a false path. The date of the document -- the number of the document, of the conclusions, is 03315/92. The Erceg one is 03316. I'm afraid they were just copied in reverse order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dzonlic. You have heard what Ms. Korner Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. pointed out, namely, that following the official number given by the authorities in the region at the time, it seems that the document containing the conclusions reached by the Crisis Staff in the meeting of the 13th of May, 1992 preceded the decision signed by Mr. Erceg. And on the basis of that, it was pointed out to you by Mr. Ackerman that what this means is that while the Crisis Staff recommended the appointment of Mr. Brdjanin as secretary of whatever it was, Nikola Erceg, president of the Executive Council, only appointed him as an acting secretary of the same section or transport and communications, or whatever it was. What do you have to state in this regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's quite clear. I wish to say that the Crisis Staff made a recommendation pursuant to item 8 that Radoslav Brdjanin is to be appointed secretary of the secretariat, and the fact is that the president of the Executive Council, Nikola Erceg, appointed him acting secretary and not secretary -- he appointed him acting secretary, which in my view is only a technical solution, an interim solution. There is no doubt that as acting secretary, he had the same authority that a secretary would have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Ackerman, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can I take it that Mr. Erceg could also remove him from this position as acting secretary when he decided to appoint a permanent secretary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You answer that question only if you are in a position to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it involves your knowledge or you knowing what the powers of Mr. Erceg as president of the Executive Council were. If you're not quite sure, you know what to do.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, Mr. Nikola Erceg, as president of the Executive Council, could replace his secretaries, the secretaries of the secretariat, whenever he wanted, because he was the president of the Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look now at paragraph 6 of document number 9. That's again conclusions of the ARK Crisis Staff of 13 May. It's the one we've been talking about with paragraph 8. We're going to move up to paragraph 6 now. It talks about certificates issued by the Crisis Staff to individuals who are moving out of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And says, "those certificates shall also be valid for their belongings, household items, furniture, and motor vehicles." That was in fact the case. People were permitted to take household items, furniture, and motor vehicles with them when they left the area, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And these travel certificates were issued to people from all three ethnicities: to Serb, Muslims, and Croats; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the travel certificates were issued to citizens of all ethnic groups. As far as I know, I do not know any citizen of Serb ethnicity who needed a travel certificate in order to move away. I even think that citizens of Serb nationality who wanted to leave were not to go and ask for travel certificates. They left in other ways, not by the same procedure that we have already explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I need the witness to be provided with a couple of documents, P295 and P242. Your Honour, I seem to have misplaced my own copy of P242. I wonder if maybe the Prosecution has an extra copy I could refer to or how we might deal with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The witness has it. I just don't have one to refer to myself. I apparently left it in my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, and as usual, it's not even the right document. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I was under the impression that last time you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am under the impression that last Friday you referred to this document, only to find out that it was not the document you wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then you told us you wanted another document, but I can't remember which other document you told us you wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I can't either. Maybe we could take the morning break now and I could get myself better organised? Would that make sense?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It would make sense to me, too. Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we can break now. In the meantime, Mr. Ackerman, please could you tell us which other documents you will be making use of? P295, as I understand, and what else?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just that, and this one that I am not able to find, and I think P43.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll break for 25 minutes, resuming at twenty to 11.00. Twenty to 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We gave you a little bit more time, Mr. Ackerman. Make sure you've got the numbers right this time. Could you bring in the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like the witness to have P43, P247, and the one we were previously referring to, which I think is P295 and P227.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. Ackerman, and what I'm going to tell you applies to everyone. I've been asked by the interpreters - very rightly so, because I apologise, but we always let them down, and this is very important for them - to ask you to slow down. And indeed you were actually firing questions a little bit too fast and too soon after the witness was finishing giving you the answer. So please slow down a little bit. And always allow a little bit of a pause between his reply and your next question. I thank you. Also, we are advised not to speak at the same time. And we'll try to be more educated. Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Trying get a bunch of lawyers not to speak at the same time may be an impossible task. We can try.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, you will have been handed to you document P43, which is an extract from the minutes of a session of the assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina of 17 July 1992. Do you have that document?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It is the 18th assembly session, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is indeed. The first thing I'll draw your attention to is that the document indicates that the assembly was presided over -- the session was presided over by Vojo Kupresanin, who chaired its work. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you go to item 2 of this extract, what I really want to point out was that proposals were presented to the assembly. Following the proposal, there was a debate in which members took part. And then a conclusion was adopted. And you'll see that in item 2 and item 3 and item 4. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Presumably, once the assembly adopted these conclusions, they were then prepared formally for the signature of Mr. Kupresanin, who was president of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the Crisis Staff would have functioned much the same way. There would have been proposals with debates, with votes, and then whatever the conclusion of the members of the Crisis Staff were, that would be formally prepared for the signature of the president. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it should be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at item 4, item 4 was a -- an agenda item regarding verification of decisions, conclusions adopted by the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And with regard to that, there was a debate. Several members took part. And then those decisions/conclusions were adopted, were they not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you know, can you tell us why the ARK Assembly was involved in verifying decisions and conclusions of the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency? Why did that happen? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the decisions have to be verified by the assembly. All decisions of bodies which perform the functions of the assembly are duty-bound to be submitted to the assembly for verification, the assembly being the highest level body, the legislative body which verifies those decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could we go now to a document which you have before you. It's P247. We saw it, I think, on Friday for the first time. I want to first draw your attention to paragraph 3A. Let me draw your attention to something else first. You had before you that -- it's P227, the gazette from ARK. And the last document in that gazette is decision number 28, right at the very end, a decision signed by Nikola Erceg. And the only thing I want to draw your attention to is that that decision was dated 5 June of 1992. Do you agree with me about that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't know exactly which document you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's at the very end of that gazette, number 28. It's the last item in that gazette.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you at least give me the number, please.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of the decision.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dated the 4th of June, 1992, on the appointment of the acting director of the radio television?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. It's the one right after that. There are two 28s, I guess. But the one right after that, the second 28, is a decision signed by Nikola Erceg.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the rates of special payment to the automobile association?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's it. All I'm really interested in is the date of that decision. 5 June, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 5 June 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now go, please, to Exhibit P247. And that exhibit is dated 14 June 1992, is it not? Just nine days later.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intermunicipality agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 14th of June, 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Which is about nine days after the last decision from the Autonomous Region of Krajina that appears in that gazette; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to -- on that document paragraph 3A. It says: "We think that the work of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina under wartime circumstances should be much more serious and that its politicians and experts should pay more attention to the problems in all constituent municipalities of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." That's what it says, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see it. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And this is a document from representatives of Srpska Krupa, Bosanski Petrovac, Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Dubica, Prijedor, Bosanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only I don't know of this town called Srpska Krupa. I know of a town called Bosanska Krupa. What about -- but Srpska Krupa, I don't know. And all the other towns, I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the same place. It's just people from Bosanska Krupa deciding it ought to be called Srpska Krupa, I'm sure. If you look at paragraph B, 3B, the document says: "We propose Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that Vojo Kupresanin be appointed president of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, given the position he currently occupies as president of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." And then it has some words, and then it can't be translated, apparently. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So this group from these municipalities apparently are wanting Kupresanin to replace Brdjanin as president of the Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that he should be replaced. They're just suggesting that he should be the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if Kupresanin is made the president, then Brdjanin probably wouldn't be the president any longer; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, if that were to be so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph F, it begins with these words: "The Serbian Democratic Party must make itself felt." And then the next paragraph: "Accordingly, personnel changes should be made in the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and with a view to urgently breaking with individuals who have decided to obstruct the work of the Serbian Democratic Party in the Autonomous Region of Krajina and to question the lofty goals which have galvanised the Serbian people." So it appears, does it not, that they are wanting the leadership of the Crisis Staff to be changed to Vojo Kupresanin because the current leadership of the Crisis Staff is not implementing the lofty goals of the SDS properly, but obstructing the work of the SDS? Isn't that what it's -- what's being said there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, there was political struggle within factions of the SDS, and this group of people wanted this, this group that submitted this request. They had such a political stance, and they wanted Mr. Kupresanin to take over, rather than Mr. Brdjanin. And I think that this is evidence of political struggle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look now, will you please, at document P295. Now, this document is the Official Gazette of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, is it not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Issue number 4, yes. And the first decision that appears is number 48, dated 9 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Issued while Brdjanin was president. And this document is five days prior to this meeting of the Sanska Una people that we were just referring to, is it not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, what I want you to do, Mr. Dzonlic, just to save time, if you'd look at the very end of this gazette, you will find that the last decision is 1 August 1992, dated 1 August, 1992, signed by Cedo Aleksic, MD. And what I'm really interested in is the date of 1 August 1992.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. I see the date, the 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. If you just look, then, from item number 48, the decision of 9 June 1992, through the rest of that gazette. Tell us if you find any other conclusion, decision, order, or document of any kind authored by Mr. Brdjanin, or that his name appears as president or anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see that. I don't see a single decision signed by Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And with that, I thank you. And that's all the questions I have of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before Madam Fauveau starts her cross-examination, I'd hate to, as it were, go back to a theme that I raised at the end of the last cross-examination. Whatever Mr. Ackerman may think of the rule at the moment, the rule is, as we discussed, that he should put his case. And on Friday, he cross-examined the witness about the speeches of Mr. Brdjanin on two bases. One is that he didn't hear them himself, or alternatively, that they were in 1993 and part of a witness statement which, in fact, was not adhered to by the witness was read to him. But that's not the point. If the case is that Mr. Brdjanin made those speeches but that they weren't heard by this gentleman or they were made in 1993 but not 1992, then fine. He's put that case. But if his case is, as I anticipate, that they were never said, those words in particular were never said by Mr. Brdjanin, then exactly the same applies to this witness as to the previous witness. It must be put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman, this is always without prejudice to the matters you raised in your motion regarding the applicability or the legality of the specific Rule, under Rule 90 that we will discuss later on. But for the time being, what do you have to state in relation to what Ms. Korner had just pointed out?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Only that I have not forgotten to ask the witness any questions that I wanted to ask him. I've completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, in that case, Your Honour, I am taking it, as I am entitled to, that there is no challenge to what this witness said he heard Mr. Brdjanin say, other than the fact it may have been said in 1993 or it was not heard by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But the actual words were used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we can proceed with the cross-examination by the Defence team for General Talic. Madam Fauveau. Now, Mr. Dzonlic, as you may have heard me say already, you are now going to be cross-examined by a different Defence team, that's the Defence team for General Talic. Madam Fauveau, may I ask you if you anticipate to finish your cross-examination today?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope so, Mr. President. But before beginning, I should like to ask for counsel from you. As Madam Korner has just said, do I have to put the same question as Mr. Ackerman, or will it otherwise be considered as -- that I do not contest something if I don't do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would rather not answer the question myself, because the matter has been raised officially and formally by Mr. Ackerman. And later on it will be decided. In the meantime --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, for my purposes, if Madam Fauveau takes the same view or rather, her case is identical to that put forward by Mr. Brdjanin on certain matters -- although I'm at a loss at the moment to know really what case has been put -- but then all she has to do is say she adopts this cross-examination, on whatever points it is, and I will take it that she also contests it. Your Honour, while I'm -- and I'm sorry, Madam Fauveau -- Your Honour, I'm somewhat concerned about that, I have to say, about Mr. Ackerman's attitude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not the only one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The real difficulty is this: As Your Honours knows, I have no doubt at all for having heard the earlier cross-examination that Mr. Brdjanin's case on these topics is "I never said those words." And Mr. Ackerman is declining, as far as I can see, to put it to the witness. And Your Honour, the difficulties is knowing what sanction Your Honour has, if it turns out, should Mr. Brdjanin give evidence, that he does deny that and it's not been put. However ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe that I can violate Rule 97 without being subjected to very severe sanctions, and I will not violate Rule 97, regardless of what Rule 90(H)(iii) seems to say. I think Rule 97 is much more binding upon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I mean, why are you bringing into play Rule 97, to be frank with you, in relation, when we are speaking of the applicability of Rule 90(H)(ii), I don't know. Because there may be instances where, in trying to do what you are required by 90(H), you may internally feel that you -- there is a chance of revealing what your client may have told you in confidence. But not necessarily so. I mean, you don't have to reveal anything of the sort. What Article -- what Rule 90(H)(ii) says is that in the cross-examination of a witness who is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party - so that's requirement number 1, the ability to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party - counsel shall put to that witness the nature of the case for that party for whom that counsel appears which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness. What you are required to do under this section is to show to the witness himself in the course of the cross-examination that either before he makes a statement in reply to your question, or during or after, that you have -- that the nature of the case of the person you are representing in this courtroom is in contradiction or appears to be in contradiction to what the witness is stating. This is the crux of the matter. You don't have to say, "It's because my client told me so." You are not requested to make affirmations as to what your client may have told you in confidence. Certainly not. But if you have reason to believe that within the material that you have in the defence of your client, you have material which is in contradiction to what the witness is stating, then in terms of Rule 90(H)(ii), you are bound to let that witness know or face the witness with that fact. I mean, why you put in play Rule 97 as if it is -- as if it is in contradiction or as if it is transdiametrically opposed to Article -- to Rule 90(H), I don't know. Because Rule 90(H) definitely does not nullify the effects of Rule 97.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I absolutely agree with Your Honour. It's faux naivete to say that this rule has nothing to do with that one. Your Honour, at the moment, my concern is, whatever Mr. Ackerman may think of this Rule, Your Honours made a ruling and Mr. Ackerman is not abiding by it. We can -- and I think if this is going to go on, because the next witness, I anticipate some of the evidence is also going to be strongly disputed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next witness is going to be very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. And if Mr. Ackerman is not prepared to put his case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Korner, I have read his statement. We are going to have a difficult session. I anticipate it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite clear what Your Honour is referring to there. But nonetheless, in respect of Mr. Brdjanin's case, if Mr. Ackerman is not going to do it, and is in our submission flouting Your Honour's ruling, oral ruling, given then I think before I call the next witness, we better deal with his motion, deal with it on an oral submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the other hand, I'm not going to press it any further at this stage because in relation to the one or two questions that you mentioned, because I am positive that if -- unless my memory is playing tricks on me, but I am pretty sure that at a certain point in time during one of last week's sittings, Mr. Ackerman did put it to a witness that Mr. Brdjanin actually never said those words. And I can remember Mr. Dzonlic replying that -- answering, "No, I heard him personally say those words."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not actually what was put. I've got the LiveNote here. It was Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. That was not Friday. This was earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, this was the first opportunity he did to cross-examine on it. I think you're thinking about the previous witness, about two witnesses ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, this is Mr. Dzonlic. What do you have by way of a transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is page 2553 of our version of LiveNote on Friday. "Q. You told us you heard Mr. Brdjanin make certain statements on the radio in 1991 and 1992, statements about Muslim people, about the numbers who should remain in the Banja Luka region. You're familiar with the statements I am referring, to are you not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you like to change your testimony about that and agree with me first of all that you didn't hear those statements but was simply told that he had made those statements. In other words, you didn't hear them direct but -- "

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I remember very vividly. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But it's not the same thing. "Other people told you about him making those statements."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think he pressed the questions further.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to, Your Honour. "No, I wouldn't like to change my testimony and I cannot agree with you that I heard it from someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you like to change your testimony and agree with me that it was only in 1993 that you heard -- you directly heard, Mr. Brdjanin or someone told you that they had heard Mr. Brdjanin say certain things on the radio? In other words, the suggestion is that even if you did hear it -- I mean, it was in 1993. And then I didn't say, when I heard him, I didn't say that he said such and such a thing in 1992, and in 1993, someone else. When I was speaking, I think we were talking about what he said in 1991. And in 1992 and 1993, as far as I can remember, in the statement I made." And so on and so forth. And then what was read to him was part of a witness statement - not adhered to by the witness when he gave evidence, I may add, but he didn't at least identify that - about Mr. Brdjanin being very frequently on the radio, TV, and in the newspapers, especially in 1993. Before that, he was obviously not considered respectable as a spokesperson of the SDS. In 1991 and 1992, he was rarely interviewed. And after a number of questions about that, he said finally, the

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: because I'm not qualified to speak about the media. All I can say is that I personally heard him on the media. Not once but several times, I heard him." Now, Your Honour, the Rule requires, in our submission, if the case for Mr. Brdjanin is that he never used those words in 1991, that he should put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. Always without prejudice, because I think we can bring this to a conclusion. I mean, always without prejudice to your motion, which will be debated and decided upon later on. But I think at this present moment, faced with the - call it whatever you like - objection, remark, or issue that has been raised by Ms. Korner, and given also the possibility that this Trial Chamber later on may -- I'm not saying that we will -- but this Trial Chamber might actually come to a conclusion adverse to what you contend or what you expect by -- or what you request in your motion, Mr. Ackerman. So I would suggest to you at this point in time to play it safe. If after having read -- after having heard what Ms. Ackerman [sic] read out from last Friday's transcript -- Ms. Korner -- Ms. Korner read out from last Friday's transcript, it appears to you that it is wise to put it to the witness that your client never uttered the words that he mentioned in his testimony, I would do it now. Always without prejudice to your motion, as stated earlier. Why risk your motion being rejected and then being faced with a situation which can no longer be remedied?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this -- this matter has become popular in the Chambers that are in trial. Apparently after Ms. Korner raised it, it was raised both in the Bosanski Samac trial and in the Galic trial. It's my understanding- and I haven't - I haven't actually looked at with any detail the transcripts - but it's my understanding in both the Galic and the Bosanski Samac trial, the Chambers ruled that failure to put your case to the witness does not preclude you in any way from contesting the issue when it comes time to put on your own case. And in addition, I can't imagine how I could contest whether or not my client made certain statements without revealing what he has told me about whether or not he made those statements, and I don't think I can do that without his consent pursuant to Rule 97 or pursuant to the ethics of my profession, which I take very seriously. And so even though you have invited me to do that, Your Honour, I must respectfully decline, pursuant to the ethics that bind me and the plain language of Rule 97.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Fauveau, you may commence your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before beginning, I should like to inform the Chamber that I adopt the cross-examination of Mr. Ackerman, particularly where he contests the statement of the witness regarding the consequences of non-response to the mobilisation call by Serb persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dzonlic, you told us that you were a member of the War Presidency of Banja Luka that was based in Zenica, Travnik, and Sanski Most. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us the composition of that War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the War Presidency was, for a while, Ibrahim Robovic. Members were Husein Basic, Atko; Zujic Emir, Novalija Amir, -- no, Sorry. He was appointed instead of Robovic to the position of president in 1993, I think it was, towards the end of 1993. Then there was Saric Imran, myself, and a lady, Jadranka. I don't know her surname. It was not the same -- the composition was not always the same. People were replaced depending on how satisfactory their work was. I can't remember any more names. Oh, yes, I do remember one more. Safedin Begovic. He, too, was a member of the War Presidency for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were all the members of this presidency of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was this lady, and she was by nationality a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So except this lady, all the other members were Muslim?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When was this War Presidency established?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived in Travnik on the 26th of February, 1993. And at that time, the presidency had already been formed, and it had its headquarters in Zenica. So I don't know exactly the date when the first presidency was set up, but it performed its functions right through until the Dayton Accords at the end of 1995, so that I assume that it may have been formed already in April 1992, or rather, 1993. No, sorry, I apologise. No. I arrived on the 26th of February, 1993, in Travnik, and the presidency had already been formed, and I don't know exactly the date of the establishment of that presidency because I was not a member of that first presidency. I became a member of the presidency after maybe half a year. So it could be in -- I became a member in July or August 1993 of that presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what were the tasks and functions of that War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to specify all the duties of the War Presidency, but I could tell you that the main duty of the War Presidency, in view of the fact that it existed ex-territorially, was to rally all citizens of Banja Luka municipality that had been expelled and who were residing in the territory of Central Bosnia, that is, Zenica, Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also told us that you were the secretary of the Assembly of the region of Banja Luka, which was also based in Travnik. What were the functions of that assembly?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was secretary of the Assembly of the district of Banja Luka. That was temporarily based in Travnik. The district were the wartime schedule of organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the assembly were the legislative body of the district, that is, the functions of the assembly were performed by the War Presidency of the district, and there was an executive body, an executive board as an executive body. I think that I cannot list all the duties of that body because there was a decree on the formation of the district, and the main task and aim and meaning was to take care of the people that had been expelled, to organise them as best as they could, to keep a record of the displaced persons. Those were the main tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were also a judge of the military tribunal in Travnik in 1993?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was from the 30th of March until, I think, the 30th of September. I was a judge of the district court of the Travnik district. And when later on I was relieved of my judicial duties and appointed to the position of secretary of the Assembly of Banja Luka district, based in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether the court in which you worked was a civil or a military court?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a district military court.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So it was a military tribunal, was it not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a military tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, attached to which army was this tribunal?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
