utterances.text: It was not formed within the scope of the army. The military court was formed by the district of Travnik. The district of Travnik. And it was not formed by the army. It was formed by the Travnik district on the basis of a decree on the formation of a district as the wartime organisational structure of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before becoming judge in this court, had you been mobilised?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived in Travnik, and I met a friend of mine who had been at the university with me. In view of the fact that a large number of judges from Travnik had left before I arrived in Travnik, they were short of staff, and I myself, at his invitation, agreed to report of the court. And in fact, that was my mobilisation. I had a wartime assignment as judge of the district military court in Travnik, and that was considered to be the post I was mobilised to.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: By which army were you mobilised?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not mobilised by the army. I was mobilised by the municipal secretariat in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me rephrase my question. What army was there in Travnik in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to stop this. But I wonder where we are going. We're well into 1993 now and out of the period --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know, Ms. Korner. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Madam Fauveau would like to explain the relevance perhaps very briefly. But at the moment, I can't see the relevance as to what army he was mobilised in in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Fauveau, I had a big temptation of stopping you earlier, actually, when you were continually putting questions referring to the period following witness's arrival in Travnik. Perhaps at this point in time, before we can decide whether you can go ahead asking questions relative to this period, you could tell us what the relevance of the sequence of the questions -- your sequence of questions is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the questions relative to the War Presidency, I wanted to show that the Muslims and the Croats had their own War Presidency. As for the last question, I will move on. But I think at the end of my cross-examination it will be quite clear why I put this question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall move on to the mobilisation which took place in September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that the mobilisation was decided in 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In September 1991, was Bosnia still a part of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that earlier on during my cross-examination. I can repeat what I said then. Bosnia and Herzegovina was a part at the time, but of the so-called rump Yugoslavia, because the republics of Croatia and Slovenia had acquired independence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when Slovenia and Croatia acquired independence and were recognised as such?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was -- I don't know the exact date, but I think in September -- before September 1991. I don't know the date. But it was in the course of 1991, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that Croatia and Slovenia were recognised as independent states on the 15th of January, 1992? You don't know, or you're saying that that is not true?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think they were independent in 1991 already. I don't know about this date, the 15th of January, 1992. As far as I know, they acquired independence in 1991. But I don't know about this -- it's possible. I just think it was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that failing to respond to the call for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mobilisation was considered a criminal act?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that quite a number of people who did not respond to the mobilisation lost their jobs.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991, there were two labour codes in force, a federal one and a republican one, employment laws?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a law on labour relations of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I know that there was a law on basic rights stemming from employment. So there were two laws. Now, which was at the republic or the federal level, I can't say. But there were not two identical laws at the federal and the republic level. One was the law on labour relations and one was the law on basic rights stemming from employment, as far as I can now recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to suggest to you that the Law on Basic Rights Stemming from Employment was a federal law, would you be -- would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that two laws envisaged measures for the termination of employment?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that according to the federal law on employment, non-respect of National Defence obligations involved the termination of employment?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that failure to respond to mobilisation according to the law on basic rights stemming from employment resulted in termination of employment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 9 of your statement in October of 2000, you said that the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina decided that it was responsible for mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Could you tell me, please, which date? Your statement of which date?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is the statement of October 2000, page 9.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have received it in English. I do know that the government -- I'm sorry. I got my statement in English. Oh, here it is in Bosnian. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm told he should have the B/C/S version in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's page 9, paragraph 1, the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I think that it is not the same page in my Bosnian version as the one you are mentioning -- in Serbian. In any event, I stated, and said, as far as I can now remember, that the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina took a decision, according to which, on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was only the defence ministry of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was competent for proclaiming mobilisation, and not the municipal secretariats or other institutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that that decision of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina annulled the Yugoslav federal law. It is page 9 of the Serbo-Croat version of your statement of October 2000. It is page 9, after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It starts in the Bosnian --

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- made null and void.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It starts on page 8, the last two lines of page 8 in the Serbo-Croat version, and continues then on page 9. So you should have it in front of you now. And what Madam Fauveau is referring to is obviously the last part, or the second half, of the first paragraph on page 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Mr. President, that the witness still doesn't have the right version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, we are referring -- or you are being referred to your interview or your statement following the interviews of the 11th and 12th of October of the year 2000. I also have before me the B/C/S version of that statement. And if you have the same document that I have and you look at page 9, you will see that the paragraph at the very top starts: [B/C/S phrase] That is the paragraph that Madam Fauveau is referring you to. Correct, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, that paragraph actually starts the page before. The beginning of that paragraph is on the previous page, where it states: [B/C/S phrase] Now, the relevant part of that paragraph or from that paragraph, for the purpose of Madam Fauveau's question, is the second half of the second part of the paragraph that you were reading at the top of page 9 of that document. And while the witness is thinking, Madam Fauveau, I've been asked to draw your attention and kindly ask you to pause a little bit following witness's reply until it's completely translated before you proceed with the next question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I shall take care to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You did indeed say that this decision of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina made null and void the Yugoslav law.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that a decision of a government cannot annul a law?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you that it cannot be annulled. But it can be put out of action, so to speak, because of the situation. But I do agree with you; it cannot be made null and void.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So in fact this decision of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was an illegal one.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't consider it illegal. It was passed by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina through a legal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you agree that laws and decisions of the republic have to be in accordance with the federal laws?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said previously that the federal laws at that point in time, in view of the situation -- at least, that is how they were treated -- this was no longer the state of SFRY. And from that standpoint, because it was rump, procedurally laws existed because things had still not been clearly defined, but there was a rump Yugoslavia. And I even think that the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina made the recommendation that no citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina should respond to that mobilisation, being the highest body of authority in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But in September 1991, Bosnia was still not independent.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true; it wasn't independent. But Bosnia and Herzegovina within Yugoslavia was -- had the status of an equal member. It had its own assembly, its bodies, its government, as did all the other republics of the former Yugoslavia, and it was able to pass decisions, and it was for those reasons that it took this decision as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But the decision of Bosnia-Herzegovina has to be in accordance with federal decisions and laws.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. But in reality, no, because the Yugoslav People's Army, according to the law, should have protected the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- no, sorry, the borders of SFRY. And it didn't protect the borders of SFRY. So you see there's a discrepancy between what was real and what was formal or official.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. Since you are mentioning that, when the JNA went to Slovenia and Croatia to make war, wasn't that war precisely in order to protect the borders, the boundaries, of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it didn't fight in Slovenia. It withdrew from Slovenia. And in Croatia, it captured lines that it had drawn. I'm not an expert for these things, so -- all I know is that it withdrew from Slovenia, and that in Croatia, it captured certain lines itself imagined and took up positions along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So according to you, there was no fighting in Slovenia in June 1991?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call that fighting or combat. There were just certain excesses. But in essence, it withdrew and left Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I shall move on to another subject. You said that judges of Bosniak nationality were removed because they did not respond to the order for mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of the reasons for their replacement was that one, that they didn't respond to the mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you specify whether they were removed because they didn't respond to the mobilisation or because they were of Bosniak nationality.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The judges were replaced because they did not respond to the mobilisation, and I think the President of the court was dismissed on the basis of decision that Bosniaks could not hold positions of authority. And I know that the president of the civil section of the municipal court in Banja Luka, who was a Croat by nationality, was replaced from his position as president of the civil department because he was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what was the destiny of the prosecutor of Banja Luka municipality? Was he also dismissed?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the prosecutors. But let me just add that judges, women, were dismissed on the basis of the decision that responsible positions cannot be held by Muslims because women, after all, were not obliged to respond to mobilisation. And they were replaced merely because they were Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: The municipal prosecutor, that is an important position, is it not? So I assume that prosecutors of Muslim and Croat ethnicity were also dismissed.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so, too, though I'm -- as I said, I don't know. But I assume that the same applied to them. I assume only.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Banja Luka also had a public attorney, Javni Pravobranicac. Could you explain to the Chamber the function of this public attorney.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public attorney's office is a separate and special institution of the prosecution, the judiciary. In the former socialist system, it was intended to defend the public interest, to protect the public interest, before various institutions in the name of the state bodies, as a representative of the state authority, when the interest of those authority was involved. So it represented the interests of public institutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the function of this public attorney was a very important function?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me, it's not important. But in the former system, it did have a rather important role, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could Muslims and Croats continue to hold that position?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I'm saying again, I assume that the same applied in that case too, because this applied to all institutions and then that should also apply to that institution, too. It does apply.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was the public attorney for Banja Luka municipality in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar please give the witness Defence Exhibit DB33.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that that is the resignation of the public attorney of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the date of the resignation is the 14th of May, 1993, is it not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the public attorney was Mr. Edin Hergic, was it not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Edin Hergic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that Mr. Edin Hergic, the public attorney of Banja Luka in May 1993, was a Muslim or a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Travnik in 1993, were there any Serb judges over there at the court?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were Serb judges in the court, in the building of the court, only they worked in the civil court. And the military court was housed in that building. There weren't any in the military court, but there were some in the civil court.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you give us the names of those Serb judges?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the names of the judges. I just know that -- I am not from Travnik, but people who knew them -- it was known that there were some. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the hearing last Wednesday, you spoke of a decision according to which the Serbs who were not loyal to the SDS could not hold important positions. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Loyalty was required. Only those Serbs who had expressed loyalty and patriotism could hold certain positions; I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So actually, certain people could not hold important posts, regardless of their nationality.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosniaks couldn't; the non-Serbs couldn't hold any responsible positions. As for the Serb, those who were loyal, who expressed patriotism, they could hold such positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you agree with me that the decision also applied to Serbs?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two decisions. We saw there was one decision saying that non-Serbs cannot be. And there was another decision, a separate decision, which says only loyal Serbs who have demonstrated patriotism. And as far as I remember even, there was a decision according to which it was said that the SDS was the only party that was representative of the Serb people. It is a fact that Bosniaks and Croats could not hold certain positions. As for Serbs, it was required that they manifest loyalty, patriotism. And I've already explained how they proved their loyalty and patriotism.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the hearing of the 26th of February, 2002, you said that at the time when members of Serbian defence forces appeared in Banja Luka, you thought that they were members of the regular forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my impression. Not the regular army. For me, the regular and legal army was the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But in quotation marks, one could say members of the army that was in Banja Luka, because they were wearing military uniforms. And I believed that they were people who are in the Serbian army. But I don't consider it legal, and I never considered it legal.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, speaking about the SOS, you said, "At the time I thought that these were members of the regular army, to -- as I didn't know that SOS existed. So I thought that they were indeed members of the Yugoslav People's Army." This is LiveNote, Tuesday, 26th of February. What I am interested in is when you said that "I thought," did you think at the time that they were members of the JNA, or do you think today that they were members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that they were members of the army, which was in Banja Luka. Members of that army, the army that was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said -- no, not yesterday. On Thursday, you said that you met a dozen or so men, that you referred to as "ninjas."

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how we called them, because they are the people who brought that money that we discussed a moment ago, and they were wearing such uniforms. And amongst ourselves, we called them ninjas. That's the name we gave them, because they reminded us of the ninjas from films.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: This pizzeria in which you met them, who owned this establishment?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was the owner. I just know that it may have been opened about six months or a year before that. I don't know who was the owner.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you see these men? In what period of time?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it was in 1992. I know it was warm, because we could sit outside late in the evening. So I can't tell you exactly when it was. But it was warm weather, and I think that one could sit outside until 10.00 without being cold. And it is judging by that, because it was warm, that I assume it was in the spring or the summer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were able to sit outside until 10.00 p.m. without being cold. Could you stay outside after 10.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have stayed out, but I never stayed until 10.00, and I don't think that you could even. I'm not quite sure, but I think, by then, there was the curfew already. But I would return home around 9.00. But I do know that it was warm because one could sit outside on the balcony. I remember that it was warm. That's why I'm saying it was warm. So I wouldn't stay outside after 9.00 ever.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you met these people in the pizzeria, were they disagreeable with you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not disagreeable in relation to anyone. Only, they gave me the impression that they were showing off. I don't know what the right term would be. But they weren't bullying anyone or anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was anyone else disagreeable with you in that pizzeria?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that these men had brought money from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, what was the currency in use in Banja Luka in 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dinar, the dinar, the "Yugoslav dinar," I think it was called. But it was then that they brought this new dinar, this new money in. And they said, "This will from now on be the means of payment, the new dinar." And indeed, after a short while, it was the currency in use. It was also the Yugoslav dinar, only the appearance had changed, I think. The pictures on the notes were different and maybe the bank notes -- the value of the bank notes changed. But that was the means of payment in use.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But in 1992, the official currency in Banja Luka was still the Yugoslav dinar, was it not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Even though, in reality, the Deutschmark was used most, the Deutschmark in real life, in daily dealings.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am now moving on to another subject. Perhaps this would be an appropriate moment for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. I would agree with you. We can now break for about 25 minutes, resuming at ten to 12.00, ten to 12.00 -- sorry, ten to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I return very briefly -- because obviously Mr. Dzonlic needs to come back to Rule 90(H). Your Honours actually made a ruling on the 21st of February at page 2131 of the transcript. Mr. Ackerman is actually not theoretically, but practically, flouting that ruling and says he's not going to obey it because his contention is this Rule is in breach of the Statute, and of Rule 97, which interestingly is not mentioned once in the motion that he filed. But Your Honour, it seems to me that this is clearly -- unless Your Honours are persuaded by what's -- the contents of the motion, Your Honours have very factually been invited to change your ruling. Your Honour's ruling stands, and Your Honour, what we would have to say would be identical to the way I put the case effectively when we argued it orally. It is going to have a serious effect, not only on this trial but from what Mr. Ackerman says, and I believe that's correct, on other trials as to how this Rule is applied. I was wondering -- and can I say straight away that Madam Fauveau told me they intend to file something on this matter tomorrow or this afternoon --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. But I was wondering whether in a sense whether Your Honours, having got their motion, having perhaps heard me again orally, could make a ruling. And if it is along the lines of the ruling that Your Honour has already made, then Your Honours do have power to grant us what I would call a certificate for appeal. Your Honour, it's clearly -- whichever way Your Honours rule, it's going to go to the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Rule 73(C) states that: "The Trial Chamber may certify that an interlocutory appeal during trial from a decision involving evidence or procedure is appropriate for the continuation of the trial. If such certification is given, a party may appeal to the Appeal Chamber without leave". Your Honours, I would invite Your Honours to perhaps consider the matter before we call the next witness and make a ruling. Mr. Ackerman, whatever his personal views, is obliged --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to make sure that we have the same text --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I wonder if it's been changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also, I may inform you that it is also -- what you have here is also under review. What you have here is also under review.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just -- Your Honour is quite right. It may have changed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It has. I'm sorry. I'm reading the old version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it is the amended version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Your Honours. You are quite right. The amended version reads: "The Trial Chamber may certify that an interlocutory appeal during trial from a decision involving evidence or procedure is appropriate for the continuation of the trial upon a request being made within seven days of the issuing of the decision. If such certification is given, a party may appeal to the Appeal Chamber, without leave, within seven days of the filing of the certification." Your Honours, I'm grateful. Unfortunately, I still haven't produced a printed version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also what you have here is also being -- is under review at the present moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wasn't aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There may be some further changes within a very short time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that, Your Honour. I hope it's not to abrogate the rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the next Plenary, which will be in April, probably. In April, as early as April, there may be some changes to this as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would encourage Your Honour, therefore, if the idea is to abrogate the Rule, in other words to remove it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. We're not talking of Rule 90.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Rule 73. I appreciate that

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It's going to be modified, presumably. I mean, I can't say that it the will definitely be modified. But there's some discussion going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd be grateful really because for the moment it is not enough for Mr. Ackerman to say, "I decline the oral decision that Your Honours have made."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think we have two issues here. Or before I express myself, let me hear what Mr. Ackerman has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have with me the transcript of the discussion we had previously regarding this, but it's nowhere near as clear as Ms. Korner would suggest to you it is. I recall early on in the transcript that I made the point that I should not be required to put to the witness something that could only come from my client. And Your Honour saying, "I absolutely agree with you about that." So that's in the transcript, and that's all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I said, Mr. Ackerman, "You need not tell the witness that -- or reveal that this information is forthcoming from your client." But basically, you as a lawyer, know very well that before you embark on defending someone, you have meetings and meetings and meetings, and conferences with your client, so that you are put in a position to be able to defend your client to the best of your ability. It doesn't mean to say that the moment you open your mouth and make a statement which is based on the information that your client has given you, in order to put you in a position to defend him, that you are violating the rule under 97. Of course it doesn't. It will violate if you come out here and you will say, "I had a discussion with my client, and my client told me this and told me that." That would be in blatant violation of Rule 97 and any rule of ethics by which all lawyers are -- all lawyers are bound. But telling Mr. Dzonlic as a witness: "I put it to you that you may be wrong in that these words were never uttered by my client, Mr. Brdjanin," does not mean that you are revealing necessarily what Mr. Brdjanin said or may have told you. He may have told you nothing about it. But you are there, and you have -- you have taken upon yourself the responsibility of defending your client. And what I tried to hint at you, to suggest to you before, leaving completely unprejudiced your legal rights to have Rule 90(H)(ii) contested was to play it safe and not find yourself possibly later on in a situation whereby what Ms. Korner threw in your face, in inverted commas, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. at a certain point in time would prejudice your case. I mean, because you never know how this 90(H) business is going to finish. I don't know. You don't know, and Ms. Korner doesn't know. I mean, it would be very, very pre-emptive on my part to even hint at where we could be heading. We haven't even started discussing the matter, because we are waiting for a response from the Prosecution. And now we also hear that the Defence team for General Talic is going to file a motion. So the matter is quite open, much more open than it possibly was last Friday or earlier on this morning. I see no -- absolutely no harm in taking -- I mean, the stand -- the rigid stand that you have taken, I can understand. But not when I tell you that whatever argument you may have in putting forward the motion that you have presented last week remains unprejudiced. Then I don't see any reason any more. Because what I was trying to do was to help, rather than put you in a difficult position. I mean, let's put it like this: You -- I don't know what the law is like in the United States on this particular matter. But I am sure that you know that in many common law jurisdictions, this is not unheard of. This is something that exists in many countries. And it exists precisely because the purpose, the raison d'etre, of the cross-examination varies according to jurisdictions. Over here, if you look at 90(H), the first -- the very first paragraph of 90(H), you will immediately see what was in the mind of the Judges when they introduced this new rule way back in 1999. In the first paragraph of 90(H), what we did -- I wasn't here at the time, but it's -- I belong to the team now. What we did was we specified the parameters of cross-examination, something that was needed, because unfortunately or fortunately, I don't know, we were having cases here where lawyers came from different jurisdictions and sometimes from jurisdictions where the system -- the whole system of -- or the whole concept of cross-examination does not exist. So basically you have the first rule which is common to practically all of the systems which I am aware of, where you have a cross-examination, and that is that cross-examination, on principle, should be limited to the subject matter of the evidence in chief. That is the basic rule as it obtains in all jurisdictions that I know of -- I know of where you have cross-examination. Then you have another instance, another section, where cross-examination can delve into. And that is if you, as the lawyer conducting the cross-examination, want to put questions affecting the credibility of the witness. Again, that is something that is common to most of -- or if not all the jurisdictions that I know of where you have the cross-examination system. And then finally, something that was introduced but which exists in most common law jurisdictions that I know of: Cross-examination can also get outside the parameters of the first two instances, the first two sections, in other words, the subject matter of the evidence in chief, or matters referring to credibility, if you jump out of those boundaries and you embark on a cross-examination purporting to put questions to obtain answers which are relevant to your case, the case of your client, then all of a sudden immediately the provisions of paragraph 2 of section 9(H) -- or when I say "section," pardon me. I'm used to sections and articles. I don't usually work with rules. But then immediately, automatically, the provisions of para 2 of Rule 90(H) come into play. And this is where you are required by this section if you are going to ask questions to the witness, purporting to obtain evidence from him which is relevant to your case, you have to tell him or her what your case is, number one. And secondly, that if he's saying "white," you have reason to believe that he is not saying the truth because you have evidence in your hand which says "black." This is what is required from you under 90(H), para 2, which is a logical sequence to para 1 of 90(H), and it is something that exists in many jurisdictions. If need be when we come to a decision -- we can tell you it exists in -- it exists in Singapore, it exists in the United Kingdom, it exists in Malta, it exists in several places. I don't know if it exists in the United States. I haven't checked. And to be frank with you, I have a book now which I took with me over the weekend to read but I never managed to get it to because I was reading the statements of the witnesses we will be hearing next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know that it doesn't exist in the United States or Canada. That part I'm certain of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Canada, I don't know either. But I can check very easily with Canada because I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I also know it doesn't exist in any country that's part of European Community because it would violate the European Convention of Human Rights, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's your contention. That's my contention

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's my contention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your contention in your motion is that this is in violation of the fair trial of the due process, the whole -- because you will be bound to reveal this and that, and it is in violation of your client's right to remain silent. This is the point in issue, and this is what we will decide later on when we come to the crux of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But Your Honour -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Mr. Ackerman. I mean, I'm not arguing with you. I'm just telling you the Chamber's point of view, trying to pave the way for a smoother procedure, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not just my contention. It in fact does not exist within the European Community, with the exception of the United Kingdom. And I think it's in great jeopardy because of the United Kingdom's adherence to the European Convention of Human Rights. But that is an argument for a latter time. What I say to you now is this: It may be that I don't fully understand this Rule because I've never encountered it before, but just at first glance, and later reflection, I believe that what I've said in my motion is correct. Now, what you are inviting me to do with regard to this witness, I think I have already done. I'm not flouting your decision of last Friday in any respect, I don't believe. I think I have put to the witness what it is that I am prepared to put to the witness at this point. It seems to me that it makes little difference if the information contained in a question that I put to the witness comes to me as a result of a privileged communication with my client. Whether I say this came from my client or whether I not disclose that, I think it's obvious that that's where it came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't have to say anything, Mr. Ackerman. The whole thing is this -- I mean, let me move one further step ahead and say that it may well be the case, as has been decided in other jurisdictions, that the -- putting the nature of the case of your client to the witness, it being in contradiction to the evidence given by the witness, may sometimes be implied. Sometimes -- most of the time, it needs to be expressed. But it is not excluded that it may be implied, considering the sequence of the questions that you embark upon. What I was trying to explain to you is this, that irrespective of the fact that you are contesting the validity -- the legal validity of this particular provision, for the time being, there is the provision and there is a ruling by this Trial Chamber which is binding, at least for the purposes of this trial. What Ms. Korner is suggesting or is recommending or is asking is for the Trial Chamber to apply the provisions of 73(C) so -- providing for an appeal before we even reach the stage of deciding - deciding - the motion that you have brought forward. Am I correct, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think that's what she's asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This is why I'm repeating to you, because I -- I consider the ruling -- the point raised last week, and the ruling given by this Tribunal as something which is completely different when it comes to the nature, are different to the motion or to the essence or substance of the motion that you are raising now, because what you're raising now is the intrinsic validity of one of the Rules of this Tribunal. What you raised last time was the applicability of -- or the way Rule 90(H)(ii) ought to be applied by this Tribunal. And that is what we decided on last week. On the decision tendered down verbally, orally last week. I think it is the case of you as Defence counsel, once you have the word of the Trial Chamber, that the rest remains unprejudiced, to follow according to the lines dictated by or shown by our decision and put to the witness, who has told you what he has told you and -- upon cross-examination, the nature of the case of the party. In French, if you remember, I told you that -- to me, the translation is not a literal translation. There is more sense in what is -- what appears in the French version than what appears in the English version -- to show him that you are not accepting what he is saying but that you have material in your hand which is in contradiction to what he stated. This is all that the Prosecution asked you to do and this is all that the ruling of this Trial Chamber asks you to do, if we have to follow, or if we are to follow the provisions of this -- of this paragraph. The rest remains unprejudiced. You may within a very short time convince this Trial Chamber that all in all, this provision runs counter to your client's right to remain silent. It may run counter to any other privilege which your client may have by way of a fair trial in due process. I don't know. How can I tell you before how we are going to decide that matter? I don't know. And my two colleagues don't know, because we haven't even started discussing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I'm in full agreement with what you've said, and that is that I must comply with your ruling of last Friday. Just because I'm contesting this particular provision doesn't mean I'm entitled to ignore it, because it is the law, as I stand here now, and will continue to be the law until it's changed, if it is. I find myself in a bit of a quandary and dilemma because I don't want to do something that is -- has a negative effect on my client's case, but by the same token, I don't want to do something that will hurt my client's case. So I don't know where to proceed now. I think I have done what I am required to do and what I should do in this cross-examination with regard to the provisions of this Rule. I don't think I have failed to ask any questions that this Rule would say that I should ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's your point of view. You may be right; you may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I'm right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may be wrong, depending on the final decision that there will be, if there is one, on what Article 90(H)(ii) means -- effectively means, read in conjunction in the same context as Article -- as para 1 of that provision, of that Rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I don't think that's it at all. I don't think it has anything to do with what the Rule means. It has to do with this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. But let me ask you a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Between these two cases, proceeding the way you want or you are wishing -- you wish to proceed, and proceeding the way Ms. Korner is suggesting, whereby in actual fact there is a provision made beforehand for a possible appeal against the decision that we handed down last week -- I mean, because does it make sense -- I mean -- or any logical -- is there any -- do you see any logic at all in having that decision remaining unchallenged qua the decision, the ruling of this Tribunal, dating back to the 21st of February and proceeding with the -- with the motion? I mean, to me, what makes sense is appealing that decision and pushing the other motion, too. But if that is what makes sense, then the suggestion of Ms. Korner certainly is the way -- is the way to go about it. I mean, I will -- I will pre-empt the issue before you decide whether it's the case of appealing against my ruling or our ruling of last week. I apply or bring into operation the provisions of para (C) of Rule 73. You have every opportunity to file an appeal against that decision that, ruling, while keeping in -- under consideration until we come to a final conclusion the fresh -- the new motion that you have -- that you have presented, which to me presents this -- the same -- presents for the first time a challenge to Article -- to Rule 90(H)(ii). What we had before us last week was not a challenge to -- against Article 90(H)(ii). It was a challenge to the interpretation or the way that the Prosecution pretended that particular Rule ought to be applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the record will show, Your Honour, that I suggested in my argument that it violated Article 21 of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You did. But basically what we decided was not whether it was in violation of this or that principle. What we decided was what actually that matters -- what that Rule in effect meant and how it should be applied. And the request was precisely to that effect. It's only this motion now that challenges directly the -- the Rule itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me try to make my position with regard to this particular witness as clear as I can, because I don't want there to be a misunderstanding between me and the Trial Chamber. The allegation of the Prosecution is that certain statements were made by Mr. Brdjanin during the year 1992. I have looked at or had looked at every issue of the Glas newspaper which I can get my hands on, that the witnesses all say will reflect these statements. I have a CD-ROM that has all of the material taken from the radio station that's all in B/C/S, so I cannot read every word of it, but I have people who are in the process of looking at it and have been in the process of looking at it for some time. As I stand before you today -- and that doesn't mean it won't change. But as I stand before you today, I have found not one bit of evidence either from the radio/TV material, or from the newspaper Glas that Mr. Brdjanin made any of these statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's precisely what Ms. Korner --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So -- but I cannot stand here and say to the witness, without having complete knowledge as to whether it appears in the Glas or any of these radio things, because I tell you, I have not seen every one of them yet. I haven't found every one of them yet. But as far as I know at this point, no such statements were made between April and December 1992. Now, I could turn out to be wrong. There may be a Glas that I haven't seen yet. And I don't want to challenge this witness, saying, "Isn't it true that these statements were not made at all during 1992," and then have Ms. Korner walk in with a videotape that I haven't seen or an issue of Glas and make me look like a fool.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's always a risk. Ms. Korner herself has come here saying that there are some documents which the Prosecution know the existence of but they have been unable to bring forward. No one would be in the least surprised if these documents turn up in your case sometime during this trial. It could -- I mean, what do we do then? But the whole thing is -- again, I read to you, and I invite you to read the text in French. You have to confront the witness or [French phrase]. In other words, whatever you have -- you may not have everything, and you -- no one expects you to have everything, just as no one expects he Prosecution to be in possession of all the evidence that is required to convict your client and General Talic. They may have some witnesses, but not all. You may have evidence, but not all. You may have some evidence, but not all. But if you have reason to believe -- this is what is required from you. If the -- you have asked a direct question to the witness on cross-examination purporting to obtain from him a piece of information which fits in the nature of your case. First you have to tell that witness what you are contending. Secondly, if after you have told that witness what you are contending, that witness tells you, "No, this is not light green, this is dark blue," and you have every reason to believe that he is not telling you the truth or you have evidence in your hand or material elements in your hand, elements related to your case or your client's case, which can be put -- of which the witness can be made aware of to show him that he can be contradicted, you are duty-bound to do it in terms of Rule 90(H)(ii). This is what 90(H)(ii) -- whether it's legal or not is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it's definitely got nothing to do with what your client may have told you inside your office, or wherever you meet him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I did that. I said to him, "Isn't it the case that you did not hear Mr. Brdjanin make these statements during year 1992?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the whole issue is you put two possibilities, according to Ms. Korner, to the witness. You did not put the third possibility, which to Ms. Korner is the most important. In other words: "I put it to you, Mr,. Dzonlic that you may be living an illusion, that you are completely mistaken, because the -- we can prove with the evidence that we have that these statements were never made by Mr. Brdjanin." Or you don't even go that far. You can tell the witness, "I put it to you that it is the contention -- it is the firm belief and conviction of this -- of my client that these words were never -- were never uttered by him." It's -- the thing is that you have to put it black on white with the witness that if you have asked for some information from him which fits in your case and he hasn't given it to you, then you have to tell that witness that in spite of the fact that he has answered "white," you can prove that it is black and not white. In other words, you can -- you have elements in your possession that will prove him wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can't imagine that anybody in this courtroom could in their wildest imagination believe that if I put such a question to this witness, he will say, "Oh, oh, you're right. I'm lying." I mean, when is that -- what century is that going to happen in? That's never going to happen. So what we're doing here is something that's just kind of -- it seems to me a major waste of time. I've made it very clear to Ms. Korner just a few moments ago what my position is. I have not found any of these statements in the newspaper or in the television or in the radio. That's my position. And I've stated that basically to this witness. I don't know how I can go any further. If I say to him, "Isn't it true that you're lying that Mr. Brdjanin didn't make these statements," he's just going to say, "No, I heard them. I'm telling the truth." What else could he possibly say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the situation otherwise is -- you will be worse off. Because what do you have? You have question number one and question number two, and you never put the question to the witness whether it could well be that he's completely mistaken and these words were never uttered by your client in 1992 or whenever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've done. I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You haven't. No. What you have -- what you have done, if Ms. Korner -- I don't doubt it, if Ms. Korner read the transcript correctly, the two questions that you put to the witness do not cover that part of the scenario. You never put to the witness the possibility that irrespective of 1992 or 1993, he may be completely wrong, be completely misguided and misinformed that these words were never really uttered by your client. This is the whole issue. If the question is not put, what do you have? You have a -- a question that referred to 1993 and you have an answer referring to 1993 and you also have a question relating to 1992 and you have an answer relating to 1992. But you never had a question putting into doubt whether Mr. Brdjanin uttered those words or not. And you have an answer -- a reply by the witness stating that he heard personally these words. In other words, you have a situation -- this is why such a -- a Rule is important. You have a situation whereby the statement of the witness that he personally heard these words on the radio or on TV, whether in 1992 or 1993, has not been challenged directly by you -- directly with the witness. You have never -- you haven't contested that. You have asked the witness more than one question but never put into doubt whether those words were actually stated. This is what Ms. Korner's objection is all about, and this is what the Trial Chamber is trying to obviate in your client's interest, after all, I mean, because I have no interest in making speeches here. But it seems to me that you are -- you have still not grasped the -- you have -- Ms. Korner is smiling. You have still not grasped the real import of Rule 92 -- 90(H)(ii). It's my firm belief and possibly because you don't have it in your system in your jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only -- the only issue about these statements is whether my client made these statements in 1992. And I think I asked him that. I said, "Isn't it the case that these statements were -- that you heard these statements from other people or that they were made after 1992?" I believe that's what I asked him. Isn't that what I asked him?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what -- Mr. Ackerman still doesn't grasp the point because each time we raise this point, he goes back to the privilege that his client enjoys. If Mr. Brdjanin were to give evidence - and there is no obligation on Mr. Brdjanin to give evidence by this method - and during the course of that evidence were to assert, "I never, whether it was 1991, 1992, or 1993, said no less than two or five per cent of Muslims shall stay in Banja Luka" or "they can all eat winter cabbage," which is the other one that seems to be common, then none of that has been put to the witnesses. And the first thing that is going to be said by cross-examination to Mr. Brdjanin: "You have recently invented this. This wasn't part of your defence. You're just saying whatever you want to get out of it." Now, I don't know how Mr. Ackerman is going to stop that. And the way of stopping that is by -- his client's case, whether it comes from his client or documents being put fairly and squarely. Counsel are not meant to invent defences. Counsel get defences from what their client tells them and it is not a breach of privilege to say to the witness: "I put it to you, Mr. X, that you're not telling the truth or that you're mistaken." This Rule, 97(H) is meant to stop -- Mr. Brdjanin told me in conference or Mr. Brdjanin will say this or will that. That's what he can't reveal. That's the privilege. But what it doesn't do is prevent him from putting his case. Your Honour, I'm sorry it's now taken so long again, because actually, Your Honour is right. My suggestion was going to be either we had a further part of the argument but that in actual fact, the way to resolve this really is only going to be for Mr. Ackerman either to abide properly by the ruling or to appeal the ruling Your Honour made last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, to bring matters to a conclusion, I hope, what I would suggest is that before we call the next witness, that Ms. Korner and I each have a -- a moment or whatever the Trial Chamber decides is an appropriate amount of time, to argue the motion that I have filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that we then have a decision from the Chamber as soon as possible with regard to that, that I think both of the matters need to be part of an appeals process, if there's going to be an appeal. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But that -- in the meantime, I would apply, therefore, 73(C), with regard to the ruling that we handed down last week straight away, because it also makes sense that if you're going to appeal or she is going to appeal -- I mean, it's -- let's say you lose -- you get an adverse decision on this new motion. It only makes sense if you appeal both.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Fauveau, I'm sorry to have kept you waiting. I saw you standing up. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we are discussing Rule 90(H), I wish to inform the Chamber that our conclusions relates to the difference between the English and the French version, because in the English version, counsel is obliged to confront the witness with the elements in his possession. According to my understanding of the French language - and it is not my mother tongue; I may be wrong - the elements it has in its possession are elements which counsel can submit to the witness but certainly not an element derived from a conversation with his client, because in that case, the Rule would say that he should confront the witness with the elements he is familiar with, not that he has in his possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, I don't think we can proceed any further with the discussion. Will you please make a formal request verbally for the application of Rule 73(C) being specific as to which ruling you want --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You want the certification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's not my appeal, because I abide by it. It's Your Honour's ruling which I accept and wish to have applied. It's Mr. Ackerman who does not wish to apply or submits that Your Honours ruling does not require him to put his client's case to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, then I will do it, Your Honours. I will make a formal request under Rule 73(C) that the Trial Chamber certify that an interlocutory appeal with regard to the matters decided -- I think it was last Friday -- with regard to Rule 90(H)(ii) --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That wasn't last Friday. It was much earlier than that. The 21st.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's the ruling of 21st of February of this year and the ruling starts in the unofficial transcript -- or the argument starts in the unofficial transcript at page 2. And I can't remember where the ruling is now. But it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the Rule requires that this application I'm making be made within seven days, and that time has expired. I think you can extend it and still accept the application. I'm not sure of that. But if that's the case, it should have been made by March 1, and it was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber -- upon the request by Mr. Ackerman, Defence counsel to accused Brdjanin, considering or taking into consideration in particular the debate on the import -- import of its ruling on the -- on its ruling of February 21st, 2002, on Rule 90(H)(ii), taking also into consideration the filing of a separate motion challenging -- by accused Brdjanin challenging the legality of the said Rule, deems it appropriate to allow for an interlocutory appeal, as this would evidently be necessary for the continuation of this trial. The certification under Rule 73(C) is being given also -- in spite of the fact -- or notwithstanding that more than seven days have passed or have elapsed since the issuing of the February 21st decision. So that the position, and we will soon have to stop. I think we ought to bring the witness in so that I can explain to the witness why he has been kept waiting for three quarters of an hour outside, without being heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness, may we -- may we argue the formal motion, the written motion, at the conclusion of the testimony of this witness then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May we argue what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The written motion that I filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But that's going to be argued -- I mean, I'm still waiting for the motion that Madam Fauveau will be filing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think she will file it either today or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She said today.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will file it after the hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm just wondering if it's appropriate to argue that matter tomorrow or does Ms. Korner need more time. I think the quicker we dispose of that, the better things will be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I think really it's all so tied up with the appeal that it seems to me that all those matters can be raised in the appeal and the Appeals Chamber can then look at whether or not it's in breach of the Statute. Your Honours have made a ruling, have given leave for an interlocutory appeal, and I would have thought that that's the way to go about it. I -- it personally sees to me that that is really the matter the Appeals Chamber should look at, is this Rule in breach of the Statute, and if not, how should it be applied?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Basically what Ms. Korner is very intelligently, I must say, suggesting or putting it, is that you could now avail yourself of this certification, file an appeal straight away against the decision of this Chamber of February 22nd, and the appeal would have as a ground not only what you may have argued last week or whenever we handed down our decision but also the new elements that you are bringing forward in your motion challenging the legality of Rule 90(H)(2). Because basically, if you win on that score, our decision of February 21st, although it had nothing -- it did not deal with that -- with that matter or with that -- with that matter, would fall automatically if your appeal is upheld -- is upheld. I don't know if I'm making myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're make yourself clear. I just don't know quite how I'm going to appeal a decision that's not been made, because there are matters raised in my motion to Rule 90(H)(2) after which there's no decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, what Ms. Korner is suggesting is very obvious. I mean, your motion, new motion, will remain in abeyance, so to say, because this same substance of it would be the grounds of appeal against our decision of February 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're probably right. I just need to look at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope I understood you well, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. If I am making a mistake, please tell me, because I -- sometimes things get difficult and get out of hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman made it plain in the course of the argument that his suggestion was that this Rule was in breach of the Statute. It appears in the transcript. And so one of the grounds of appeal against the decision will be on the basis that the Rule should not stand at all because it is in conflict with the Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. And perhaps because in my -- in our ruling we just mentioned you, the Trial Chamber is making it clear also that what applies to you applies also to Madam Fauveau, obviously, particularly knowing now that we know that it is the intention of General Talic to file a motion. Now, you may decide whether it's worth your while to file the motion or not, but I -- at this point in time, I would say go ahead. And on the basis of the fact that you have filed your motion, you can actually join hands with Mr. Ackerman in appealing against the February 21st decision, because you would have the same interests, even though the argument may be different, you would have the same interest. Can I have the witness, please. Mr. Dzonlic, we don't like it -- we don't like keeping witnesses waiting outside for more than it is necessary, and it was the intention of this Trial Chamber to finish with your testimony this morning. However, a legal problem has arisen which needed to be debated before we could proceed with your cross-examination. So unfortunately, we took the past three quarters of an hour discussing the legal problem involved, with the result that I apologise to you for having kept you waiting outside, not knowing exactly what was happening, and also as a result of that, you will have to come again tomorrow morning. Again, my apologies. I'm sorry, but it was not something capricious. This was something that we had to do because it was a very important legal matter -- there was an important legal matter involved. I thank you. You may now withdraw. And hopefully tomorrow morning you will finish your testimony within a very short time. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand fully, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So again, my apologies to the interpreters. Maybe also during the debate we were exchanging and -- remarks very fast. My apologies. We will meet tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: be reconvened on Tuesday, the 5th day of March, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
